---
title: "Plotting"
description: "Draw data, curves and residuals with make_plot() and make_residual_plot(), with linearising transformations and your own styling."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, out.width = "100%")
```

`make_plot()` draws data points and model curves, with or without a linearising transformation. `make_residual_plot()` draws residuals, and `update_plot_curve()` swaps the curve in an existing plot. All three return ggplot objects, so you can print them, save them, or change them further with ggplot2. [Plot types](../concepts/plots.html) explains what each transformation shows.

```{r}
library(enzKinet2)

set.seed(42)
data <- simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 0.8, Vmax = 12), x.min = 0.1, x.max = 6,
                      n.samples = 8, n.replicates = 2, noise.level = 0.05)
fit <- fit_model("MM", data, start.params = list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), get.conf.int = TRUE)
curve <- make_curve("MM", fit$fitted.params, x.min = 0.1, x.max = 6, conf.int = TRUE)
```

## Data, curves and the true curve

`data.df` is drawn as points, `curve.df` as lines, and `extra.curve` as a black line on top. All three are optional, but you need at least one of them to see anything:

```{r}
true_curve <- make_curve("MM", list(Km = 0.8, Vmax = 12), x.min = 0.1, x.max = 6)
make_plot("MM", data.df = data, curve.df = curve, extra.curve = true_curve,
          x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min")
```

Here the coloured line is the fit and the black line is the curve the data was simulated from. EKA2 uses `extra.curve` for its "true curve" option.

## The envelope

With `conf.int = TRUE`, `make_plot()` shades the parameter uncertainty envelope between the lower and upper curves. The curve must come from `make_curve(..., conf.int = TRUE)`, which needs the confidence bounds that `fit_model()` returns:

```{r}
make_plot("MM", data.df = data, curve.df = curve, conf.int = TRUE,
          x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min")
```

The envelope shows how far the curve moves when each parameter is at the edge of its confidence interval. It is not a confidence band for the curve: see [Fitting and confidence intervals](../concepts/fitting.html).

## Transformations

`plot.transformation` redraws the same data and curve on different axes. The curve is transformed with the data, so you always see the fitted model, never a straight line fitted to the transformed points.

```{r, fig.height = 3.6}
for (transformation in c("log10", "lineweaver", "hanes", "eadie")) {
  print(make_plot("MM", data.df = data, curve.df = curve, conf.int = TRUE,
                  plot.transformation = transformation))
}
```

- `"log10"`: v against log10(a).
- `"lineweaver"`: the Lineweaver-Burk plot, 1/v against 1/a. Each curve is extended to the horizontal axis (for Michaelis-Menten it crosses at −1/Km), and a dotted line marks 1/a = 0.
- `"hanes"`: the Hanes plot, a/v against a.
- `"eadie"`: the Eadie-Hofstee plot, v against v/a. The envelope isn't drawn on this plot, even with `conf.int = TRUE`: v is on both axes, so the envelope's curves move sideways as well as up and down, and can't be shaded as a band.

### The direct linear plot

`"direct"` draws the direct linear plot, for Michaelis-Menten only. Each data point (a, v) becomes a line through (−a, 0) and (0, v), in axes of Km and Vmax. The lines cross near the best estimates:

```{r}
make_plot("MM", data.df = data, plot.transformation = "direct")
```

It needs `data.df`, and it doesn't draw curves (it warns if you pass one). Points with a concentration of 0 have no line.

### Points that can't be transformed

A transformation can turn a point into an infinite value, such as 1/a at a = 0. Such points are dropped with a warning:

```{r}
curve_from_zero <- make_curve("MM", fit$fitted.params, x.min = 0, x.max = 6)
p <- make_plot("MM", curve.df = curve_from_zero, plot.transformation = "lineweaver")
```

To avoid it, start curves for the log10, Lineweaver-Burk, Hanes and Eadie-Hofstee plots just above 0, as above.

### Which models allow which plots

Not every transformation makes sense for every model. This table comes from `BLOCKED_TRANSFORMATIONS`:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
blocked <- vapply(VALID_MODELS, function(m) {
  b <- BLOCKED_TRANSFORMATIONS[[m]]
  if (length(b) == 0) "none" else paste(b, collapse = ", ")
}, character(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Code = VALID_MODELS, Model = unlist(PLOT_TITLES[VALID_MODELS]),
                        `Not allowed` = blocked, check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

Only Michaelis-Menten allows the direct linear plot. Substrate inhibition, Hill and the binding models only allow the standard and log10 plots. Asking for a blocked transformation is an error.

## Axis units

`x.units` and `y.units` are the units of the raw variables. The axis labels show the units of what is plotted, so a Lineweaver-Burk plot gets reciprocal units:

```{r}
make_plot("MM", data.df = data, curve.df = curve, plot.transformation = "lineweaver",
          x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min")
```

The Hanes y-axis (a/v) and the Eadie-Hofstee x-axis (v/a) get combined units in the same way. The log10 x-axis has no units.

## Labels, title, legend and style

The other arguments change the text and look:

```{r}
set.seed(3)
inhibition <- simulate_data("NCI", list(Km = 0.8, Vmax = 12, Ki = 2), x.min = 0.2, x.max = 6,
                            n.samples = 6, z.values = c(0, 1, 3))
make_plot("NCI", data.df = inhibition,
          curve.df = make_curve("NCI", list(Km = 0.8, Vmax = 12, Ki = 2), x.min = 0, x.max = 6,
                                z.values = c(0, 1, 3)),
          x.label = "Glucose", y.label = "Rate", x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min",
          title = "Non-competitive inhibition", legend.label = "Inhibitor (mM)",
          palette = "Dark2", show.grid = TRUE, y.range = c(0, 12))
```

- `x.label`, `y.label` and `title` replace the defaults. Units are still added to the labels.
- Models with an extra variable (`I`, `B` or `R`) get one colour per value, and a legend. `legend.label` replaces the legend's default title, and `hide.legend = TRUE` hides it. Models without an extra variable are drawn in one colour with no legend.
- `palette` is a ColorBrewer palette from `PLOT_COLOUR_PALETTES` (default `"Set1"`). If it has fewer colours than there are values to colour, ggplot2's default colours are used instead.
- `show.grid = TRUE` adds grid lines.
- `y.range` fixes the y-axis limits. Points and curves outside them aren't drawn.

### Binding models

For the binding models the dependent variable is a fraction bound, so the y-axis shows 0 to 1 unless you set `y.range`:

```{r}
make_plot("BK", curve.df = make_curve("BK", list(KD = 2), x.min = 0, x.max = 20),
          x.units = "µM")
```

## Customising and saving

Since the result is a ggplot object, you can add any ggplot2 layer, scale or theme to it:

```{r}
make_plot("MM", data.df = data, curve.df = curve, conf.int = TRUE,
          x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw() +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 12, linetype = "dashed")
```

Save a plot with `ggplot2::ggsave()`:

```{r}
p <- make_plot("MM", data.df = data, curve.df = curve, x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min")
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
ggplot2::ggsave(file, p, width = 15, height = 10, units = "cm", dpi = 300)
```

Use a `.pdf` or `.svg` file name for a vector image.

## Replacing a plot's curve

`update_plot_curve()` removes the curves and envelope from a plot made by `make_plot()` and draws new ones, keeping the data points. Pass the same model, transformation and palette that the plot was made with:

```{r}
p <- make_plot("MM", data.df = data,
               curve.df = make_curve("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0.1, x.max = 6))
update_plot_curve("MM", p, curve.df = curve, conf.int = TRUE)
```

This is useful when you redraw a plot many times, for example as parameter values change.

## Residual plots

`make_residual_plot()` plots the data minus the model's prediction at each point, against the concentration. It takes the parameter values directly, not a curve:

```{r}
make_residual_plot("MM", fit$fitted.params, data, x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min")
```

Residuals from a good fit scatter evenly around zero. A pattern, such as residuals mostly on one side of zero or following a curve, means the model or its parameter values don't describe the data:

```{r}
make_residual_plot("MM", list(Km = 1.5, Vmax = 13), data, x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min",
                   title = "Residuals from parameter values that don't fit")
```

Its options mostly match `make_plot()`'s:

- By default the y-axis is centred on zero and just covers the largest residual. `y.range` sets it instead.
- The x-axis starts at 0 and covers all the data. `x.max` extends it further, for example to line it up with a plot of the curve.
- `zero.line = FALSE` removes the dotted line at zero.
- `x.label`, `y.label`, `x.units`, `y.units`, `title`, `legend.label`, `palette`, `hide.legend` and `show.grid` work as in `make_plot()`. Here `y.units` are the residuals' units, the same as the dependent variable's.
